title: The king and his sons (Kern ch. 25)
hook: two princes lead their father to the teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chapter of the Lotus that people chant on its own, the chapter of Guanyin who hears the world's cries. Your line: chanted everywhere. Did a line of it come back to you? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

Two young princes want to go and hear a Buddha teach. Their father, the king, follows a different teaching and isn't interested. So the boys go to their mother first. Her advice is unexpected. Don't sneak off, she says, and don't argue with him. Go to your father, and show him something. Let him see, so his mind turns clear. That's the setup of chapter twenty-five of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering. It's a family story, set in a past age, and it runs backward from the way families usually work. Today: the king and his sons.
screen: `TWO PRINCES WANT TO GO.` → `THEIR FATHER ISN'T INTERESTED.` → `THEIR MOTHER SAYS: SHOW HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's what the sons do, as the chapter tells it. They rise into the air in front of their father, and they walk there, sit there, lie down there, as if the sky were a floor. Water and fire stream from their bodies. They grow vast, then small again. The king is astonished, and glad. Who taught you this, he asks. Who is your teacher? And the sons answer: a Buddha, teaching the Lotus not far from here. The king says, then I want to see him too. Notice the direction. We usually expect teaching to flow downhill, from parent to child. Here it runs uphill. The sons don't lecture their father into anything. They show him, and let him ask. The sons also ask their parents' leave to become monks, and the chapter gives a picture for how rare it is to meet a Buddha: like a turtle adrift on the ocean, surfacing right into the hole of a floating log. Then the whole family goes. The king hears the teaching, and in time he leaves his throne to practice. And here's the line that gives the chapter its heart. The king says to the Buddha that his two sons have been his good friends. They turned him around. The Buddha agrees, and says that a good friend is a great cause: the one who leads another to see a Buddha and to set out on the path. The chapter ends with a reveal. The Buddha tells the assembly who these people became, and the two sons are the Medicine King, whose story we heard a few days ago, and his brother. A good friend, in this sutra, can be your own child.
screen: `THE SONS WALK ON THE AIR.` · `WHO IS YOUR TEACHER?` · `A TURTLE AND A FLOATING LOG.` · `MY SONS ARE MY GOOD FRIENDS.` · then, large: `THE SONS LED THE KING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: learn from someone younger. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone younger than you. A child, a niece, a student, the new person at work, a neighbor's kid. Now find one thing they know, or see, or do better than you do. Maybe it's small: a shortcut on a phone, a way of saying sorry quickly, a song. Maybe it's not small at all. Just let it be true for a minute that they could lead you somewhere. If nothing comes, stay with the breath, and let someone come to mind later today. The bell holds the time.
The king and his sons. A father led to the teaching by his own children, who showed him instead of arguing. Today's word.
screen: `THE KING AND HIS SONS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the sons led the king. Today, ask someone younger to show you one thing, and let them lead without correcting them. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter is taught as a story about the good friend, the person who leads another toward the teaching, and it ties back to the Medicine King chapter, since the two princes are revealed to be the Medicine King and his brother.

fork.setup: you're one of the two princes. you want to hear the Buddha, and your father follows a different teaching. what do you do?
options: go to him and show him something he can see.
fork.reveal: on their mother's advice, the sons go to their father and show him wonders in the air. he's glad, and asks who taught them.

original.note: Sanskrit: a good friend, someone who helps another toward the path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy tale about magic princes.
what it means: two sons show their father wonders instead of arguing, and lead him to the Buddha; he calls them his good friends.
what a scholar hears: the chapter turns on the good friend, kalyanamitra, and ties back to the Medicine King, who it reveals was one of the sons.

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 25, not quoted. Names left out of the voice (King Subhavyuha, Queen Vimaladatta, sons Vimalagarbha and Vimalanetra in Kern); confirm whether to add them.
'Follows a different teaching': Kern has the king devoted to the brahmans / other doctrines. Phrased neutrally on purpose so no tradition is the foil; confirm.
Wonders paraphrased: walking, sitting and lying in the air, water and fire from their bodies, growing large and small. Confirm against Kern.
The one-eyed turtle and floating log image: confirm it appears in this chapter in Kern's version (it is in Kumarajiva's Chinese). Also the udumbara flower image, not used.
Good friend as 'a great cause': confirm the wording in Kern.
Reveal: the two sons are Bhaishajyaraja (Medicine King) and Bhaishajyasamudgata; confirm for Kern's version. Tied to day 1178.
Kalyanamitra (कल्याणमित्र) as the original-language word: confirm it is the term used in this chapter.
Editor: dropped 'one-eyed' from the turtle image (voice and match pair), since that detail is Kumarajiva's and not confirmed for Kern's version cited here.
